frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and pipeline infrastructure, but European demand, pricing, and the energy transition constrain long-term leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Morocco-Western Sahara Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The dispute with Morocco continues to shape defense spending, regional diplomacy, and competing transport and energy corridors across North and West Africa.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: US, European, and Chinese interest in the Lobito corridor and nearby critical-mineral supply chains creates investment opportunities but could dilute Angolan control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Legacy oil-backed financing and dependence on offshore petroleum leave Luanda vulnerable to commodity-price swings and external creditors despite diversification efforts.

highlights: Cotonou remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: Niger Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Tensions over the Niger-Benin oil-export route expose Benin's dependence on cross-border infrastructure and the political leverage of neighboring producers and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Sahelian Militancy Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence from the Sahel is pressuring northern Benin, increasing reliance on foreign security assistance and threatening roads, parks, and border commerce.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains significant influence through Debswana, but reliance on De Beers marketing channels and weak global diamond demand limits sovereign control over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Water Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Power imports, coal dependence, and water scarcity create openings for external infrastructure financiers while complicating efforts to develop domestic mineral processing.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Control
frictionVectors.details: The junta is tightening state oversight of industrial and artisanal gold, but weak enforcement and informal extraction continue to limit effective national control over revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's expanding security relationship with Russia reduces Western influence but may create new dependencies involving military assistance, mining access, and opaque commercial arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control and value addition in its mining sector, but limited capital and processing capacity leave it dependent on foreign investors and commodity buyers.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain a major sovereignty risk, with accusations surrounding armed groups and cross-border insecurity constraining trade, security planning, and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Influence
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its location for ports, maritime security, and logistics, but dependence on external finance and operators creates sensitivity around strategic infrastructure control.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on tourism, imported fuel, and climate-sensitive infrastructure limits economic autonomy and exposes the archipelago to external shocks and creditor influence.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain central to hydrocarbons, mining, and large infrastructure projects, while weak transparency and limited domestic processing reduce Cameroon’s ability to retain resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Persistent conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside instability near Nigeria and the Central African Republic, diverts state capacity and complicates transport and energy development.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Russian-linked security support has expanded external influence over political protection and access to gold and diamond networks, limiting transparent national control.

frictionVectors.title: Transport Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The country’s dependence on routes through Cameroon and neighboring states leaves fuel, trade, and humanitarian access vulnerable to armed groups, border controls, and foreign logistical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the fiscal backbone, but foreign technical expertise, export infrastructure, and volatile prices constrain Chad’s control over the full value chain and public finances.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s strategic position near Sudan, Libya, and the Central African Republic attracts competing foreign security interests, while regional conflict increases pressure on its military and sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: French security and territorial leverage
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved status of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute, while France retains substantial influence over security, migration management, and monetary arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence and maritime access
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic productive capacity leaves Comoros dependent on remittances, imported energy, and external financing, constraining autonomous control over ports and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals attract intense Chinese, Western, Gulf, and regional competition, while weak oversight limits the state's ability to capture value and enforce contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern armed-group and regional pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed actors continues to undermine sovereignty in the east, with alleged external support networks and contested border corridors complicating Kinshasa's control.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state's fiscal position remains heavily exposed to oil production and foreign operators, leaving public investment and sovereignty vulnerable to price cycles and contract asymmetries.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, telecommunications, and other projects expand connectivity but increase dependence on external finance, contractors, and opaque repayment or concession arrangements.

highlights: Cocoa and mining value chains diversify

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa-sector value capture
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire retains significant influence through regulation and domestic processing ambitions, but global traders and volatile prices still capture much of the cocoa value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and other investors compete for ports, logistics, energy, and mining projects, creating opportunities for diversification while testing Abidjan's procurement and debt discipline.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military basing
frictionVectors.details: U.S., French, Chinese, Japanese, and other military presences provide revenue and diplomatic weight but constrain strategic autonomy and make Djibouti vulnerable to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt concentration
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on externally financed port infrastructure and Ethiopia-linked transit exposes the economy to debt, concession, and regional trade risks despite Djibouti's pivotal location.

highlights: Suez remains a strategic revenue anchor

frictionVectors.title: External financing and asset sales
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions, Gulf deposits, and major privatizations increase foreign leverage over strategic assets and economic policy. Debt-service needs limit Cairo's room to defend full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains Egypt's central resource-security concern. Cairo continues diplomatic pressure while avoiding an open regional escalation.

highlights: Malabo pivots toward gas and offshore logistics

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field production leaves the state dependent on foreign energy companies, technical expertise, and external financing to sustain revenue. Resource governance remains highly centralized and opaque.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external partners remain important to ports, roads, and energy projects. These relationships expand connectivity but can create repayment, ownership, and strategic-access risks.

highlights: Red Sea geography raises strategic value
Mining remains the main export engine

frictionVectors.title: Regional military entanglement
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's location near the Bab el-Mandeb exposes it to competition among Gulf states, Türkiye, Egypt, and other Red Sea actors. Its security posture and ties with Ethiopia remain a persistent source of regional uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper, zinc, and gold projects rely on foreign capital and operators, limiting domestic control over technical capacity and export chains. Sanctions history and governance concerns continue to constrain diversification.

highlights: South Africa remains the economic lifeline
Sugar and manufacturing face external exposure

frictionVectors.title: South African dependency
frictionVectors.details: Trade, energy, transport corridors, and customs revenue are closely tied to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. Disruptions or policy changes there can rapidly affect Eswatini's fiscal and resource security.

frictionVectors.title: External market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, apparel, and light manufacturing depend heavily on preferential access to foreign markets and imported inputs. Changes in trade preferences or labor standards could weaken domestic bargaining power.

highlights: Port access remains a strategic vulnerability

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access competition
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Ethiopia is pursuing diversified port and logistics arrangements with Djibouti, Somaliland, and other regional partners. These efforts carry sovereignty risks and have intensified tensions with Somalia and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF engagement, and reliance on Chinese and Gulf-linked capital constrain Addis Ababa's autonomy over major infrastructure and resource projects. Internal conflict further complicates revenue collection and project security.

highlights: Military-led transition seeks tighter control over oil and mining
France recalibrates influence as Gulf and Asian investors expand

frictionVectors.title: Manganese and oil contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is pressing for greater local value addition and state participation, creating uncertainty for established foreign operators. Revenue gains remain constrained by governance and infrastructure limitations.

frictionVectors.title: Railway and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors remain vulnerable to aging rail infrastructure and concentrated port access. Chinese, French, and Gulf-linked financing could improve capacity while increasing external leverage.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty rests heavily on Senegalese security support
Fisheries, tourism, and aid remain exposed to outside market power

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked security and border dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies on regional cooperation, especially with Senegal, for security and trade access. This supports stability but narrows Banjul's room for independent strategic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign access to fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign fleets and limited enforcement threaten domestic food security and coastal livelihoods. Weak monitoring capacity reduces the government's ability to capture the full value of marine resources.

highlights: Debt restructuring is narrowing policy autonomy
Gold, oil, and critical-mineral policy are moving toward stronger state oversight

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stabilization requirements constrain public investment and reduce Accra's flexibility in managing strategic assets. Debt-service pressures continue to shape resource and infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and gold governance
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining damages land and water while diverting value from formal state channels. Foreign-linked trading networks and weak enforcement complicate efforts to secure sovereign control over the sector.

highlights: The junta is centralizing control over bauxite and the Simandou corridor
Resource nationalism is rising faster than institutional accountability

frictionVectors.title: Simandou infrastructure bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The government is using rail, port, and mining approvals to demand greater domestic benefits from foreign consortia. Chinese and other external financiers remain pivotal, limiting full strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite enclave economics
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports generate substantial foreign involvement but limited local processing and employment gains. Contract opacity and military rule heighten risks of unequal revenue distribution.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy vulnerable to external price setters
Political fragility limits control over ports, fisheries, and territory

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Farmers and state revenues depend heavily on a single commodity whose processing and pricing are largely controlled outside the country. Weak storage, finance, and processing capacity reduce domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port, fisheries, and maritime routes are vulnerable to foreign commercial pressure and illicit trafficking. Limited state capacity and recurring political instability make external security partnerships difficult to manage sovereignly.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and major external creditors constrain Nairobi's policy space. Chinese-backed transport infrastructure remains economically important while raising questions about repayment exposure and strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu corridor and emerging mineral prospects attract Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional interest. Security threats and local land concerns complicate efforts to convert infrastructure into sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water revenues and infrastructure are closely tied to South African demand, financing, and technical control. Delays and cost disputes can weaken Maseru's bargaining position over a nationally strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: Economic exposure to South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, employment, remittances, and customs revenues are heavily linked to South Africa. This dependence limits Lesotho's room to diversify partnerships or resist regional pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Large mining concessions and export corridors generate revenue but leave Liberia dependent on foreign capital, commodity prices, and concession operators. Local-content and renegotiation demands remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia and mineral-linked transport infrastructure attract competing Western, Chinese, and regional interests. Weak infrastructure and limited state oversight reduce Liberia's ability to capture full strategic value.

frictionVectors.title: Oil blockade and institutional rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities and armed groups can disrupt production, exports, and budget flows through the National Oil Corporation. Fragmented control prevents consistent sovereign management of hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, Gulf actors, and European states pursue competing security and energy interests. Their support networks deepen Libya's fragmentation and complicate control of ports, bases, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and ilmenite projects depend heavily on foreign firms, offtake agreements, and imported technology. Fiscal benefits are significant but the state retains limited control over processing and value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridors and local consent
frictionVectors.details: Large projects and associated roads, ports, and power systems can trigger land and environmental disputes. Weak grid capacity and regulatory enforcement increase dependence on private infrastructure providers.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Mining-for-finance pressure
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking external investment in uranium, rare earths and other minerals while fiscal distress limits its bargaining leverage. Licensing and revenue-sharing arrangements remain vulnerable to creditor and investor pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and fuel dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity shortages and reliance on imported fuel expose Malawi to external supply shocks. Hydropower vulnerability and limited grid investment constrain sovereign economic planning.

highlights: Junta asserts control over gold resources
Russian security ties deepen strategic dependence

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state participation and revenue shares, creating legal and operational disputes. The government’s resource-nationalist stance improves fiscal claims but risks deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security realignment
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and reliance on Russian-linked security support have reduced outside political conditionality while increasing dependence on a narrower partner base. Insecurity continues to threaten transport corridors and mining zones.

highlights: Offshore gas moves from promise to production
Nouakchott balances Europe, Gulf and China ties

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major export and domestic-energy opportunities but leaves Mauritania dependent on foreign operators, financing and cross-border coordination. Revenue transparency and local-content expectations remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore logistics bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Mauritania’s mineral economy depends heavily on the state rail system and the Nouadhibou export corridor. Aging infrastructure and external demand concentration limit the country’s control over value capture.

highlights: Services economy remains resilient but exposed

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty transition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius’s claim to the Chagos Archipelago has strengthened its sovereignty position, but implementation of any UK agreement and the future of the Diego Garcia base remain strategically sensitive. Great-power competition limits Port Louis’s room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized energy security
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius remains highly dependent on imported fuel and vulnerable to shipping disruptions. Renewable-energy expansion is progressing, but grid constraints and financing needs keep the island exposed to external suppliers.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables reinforce strategic autonomy
Western Sahara diplomacy drives investment access

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses control of Western Sahara and its phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy potential to deepen ties with partners recognizing or accommodating its position. Disputes with Algeria and legal challenges in European markets remain persistent risks.

frictionVectors.title: Green-hydrogen dependency
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is positioning itself as a major exporter of green energy and low-carbon industrial products, but projects depend on European demand, foreign technology and large external capital commitments. Water scarcity adds a domestic sovereignty constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led LNG projects remain exposed to insurgent violence and require sustained external security support. Delayed production limits Mozambique's bargaining power and fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: South African, Chinese, Gulf, and regional interests compete around Maputo and northern transport infrastructure. Concession structures may generate revenue while limiting durable domestic control.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen raise strategic stakes

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have attracted major international operators, creating pressure for favorable fiscal terms while Namibia seeks greater local participation and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Weak domestic infrastructure could leave Namibia hosting externally controlled production chains.

highlights: Junta tightens control over extractive assets

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are challenging established French-linked mining arrangements and seeking more state control. Political confrontation and legal uncertainty risk reducing output and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Growing reliance on Russian security assistance increases strategic dependence while Western sanctions and regional isolation restrict financing, logistics, and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Security and Oil Theft
frictionVectors.details: Sabotage, theft, and insecurity continue to erode state control over production and export revenues. International operators retain substantial influence because domestic infrastructure and enforcement remain uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Refining Capital
frictionVectors.details: New refining capacity can reduce dependence on imported fuels, but gas expansion still requires foreign finance, technology, and export infrastructure. Contract stability remains contested amid reform and currency pressures.

highlights: Mineral diplomacy collides with regional war

frictionVectors.title: Conflict Minerals and Eastern Congo
frictionVectors.details: Accusations that Rwanda enables mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo create major diplomatic and sanctions exposure. Regional conflict can disrupt Kigali's access to trade corridors and external markets.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control over infrastructure and mining policy but remains dependent on aid, development finance, and foreign investment. Fiscal pressure limits its room to reject external conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea maritime dependence
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe relies heavily on external partners for maritime surveillance, fisheries enforcement, and naval security. Limited state capacity leaves its offshore resources vulnerable to foreign commercial and security influence.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: External interest in ports, logistics, and connectivity offers revenue opportunities but could narrow the government's room to manage strategic assets independently.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Dakar is seeking greater domestic value capture and tighter oversight of offshore hydrocarbons, creating friction with international operators and financiers. The challenge is balancing sovereign control with production stability and investment needs.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Transport, energy, and digital infrastructure remain dependent on external capital, including Gulf, Chinese, European, and multilateral financing. Debt terms and strategic access are increasingly tied to Senegal's resource and logistics ambitions.

highlights: Blue economy remains the sovereignty core

frictionVectors.title: Maritime surveillance reliance
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on partners such as India, France, and other maritime-security providers to monitor its vast exclusive economic zone. This improves protection against illegal fishing but creates persistent sensitivity over foreign military access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, fisheries, and port infrastructure remain exposed to external financing and global shocks. Victoria must balance Chinese, Indian, European, and multilateral engagement without allowing any partner to dominate critical maritime assets.

highlights: Iron ore drives renewed strategic interest
Mining governance remains the sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-controlled mining value chains
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mineral projects generate export revenue but leave Sierra Leone exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and limited domestic processing. Contract transparency, taxation, and local-content enforcement remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining exports rely on externally financed rail, port, and logistics systems, giving operators and creditors leverage over national infrastructure. Freetown is seeking more local benefit while avoiding disruptions that could deter investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port access and regional rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf actors, Ethiopia, and other partners compete for influence over Somali ports, security arrangements, and maritime access. These deals can provide infrastructure and revenue but also risk fragmenting federal authority and strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resources and fisheries governance
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas licensing, along with fisheries access, is constrained by insecurity, weak enforcement, and disputes between federal and regional authorities. Foreign firms and security partners may gain disproportionate influence before Somalia develops robust regulatory capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater local beneficiation and strategic control over platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains. Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors are competing for access while domestic policy remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and freight bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and constrained rail and port capacity continue to limit industrial sovereignty and mineral exports. Reform is advancing, but private investment has not yet fully offset state infrastructure weaknesses.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil revenues depend on export infrastructure crossing war-torn Sudan, leaving production, transit fees, and public finances vulnerable to disruption. External oil firms and regional intermediaries retain substantial leverage over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and regional competition
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and delayed democratic milestones weaken national control over oil, land, and infrastructure. Uganda, Sudan, Gulf actors, and international donors remain influential through security, trade, and humanitarian channels.

frictionVectors.title: Gold war economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance competing armed networks, with foreign buyers and regional intermediaries capturing value outside transparent state institutions. This deepens fiscal fragmentation and weakens civilian sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and related maritime corridors are strategically important to Gulf, Egyptian, Turkish, and Russian interests. The conflict increases the risk that access agreements and infrastructure concessions will be negotiated by armed factions rather than a legitimate national government.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is using Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors to expand regional influence and reduce dependence on alternative routes. Chinese, Gulf, Indian, and Western capital is increasing, creating leverage concerns around ports, rail, and logistics concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for local processing and stronger state participation in gold, nickel, graphite, and rare-earth projects. Negotiations with multinational firms are improving fiscal control but may generate regulatory friction and investor uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Port sovereignty and concession exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's position as a transit hub for the Sahel, but dependence on foreign operators, financiers, and shipping networks limits fully sovereign control over strategic logistics. Competition among Gulf, European, and Asian actors is intensifying.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability across Burkina Faso and northern Ghana are increasing pressure on Togo's northern border and transport corridors. Security cooperation with external partners is expanding, while the government seeks to avoid excessive dependence on any single sponsor.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and political engagement remain closely tied to Tunisia’s migration controls and macroeconomic stabilization, limiting room for independent bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and phosphate vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on imported energy despite the TransMed corridor, while aging phosphate infrastructure restricts the state’s ability to capture greater value from a strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP sovereignty and environmental conflict
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline gives Kampala export infrastructure but leaves the project dependent on foreign operators, lenders, and transit arrangements amid sustained environmental and displacement criticism.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects strengthen infrastructure capacity while increasing exposure to creditor leverage and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Copper value-capture contest
frictionVectors.details: New investment from Western, Gulf, and Chinese-linked firms is expanding production, but Zambia still faces pressure to secure better taxation, processing, and local-supply terms.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring offers fiscal relief but preserves substantial influence for official creditors and private lenders over infrastructure and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum external dominance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and other foreign investors dominate major lithium and platinum projects, while limited domestic processing keeps Zimbabwe from capturing the full strategic value of its mineral base.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and alternative-finance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions constrain conventional capital access, pushing Harare toward Chinese, Russian, and regional channels that provide financing but may reduce transparency and bargaining leverage.
